summary: We put eight models in 954 cage matches to test whether the best model always wins. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash won the heavyweight class despite not having the strongest answers.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


We put eight models in 954 cage matches to test whether the best model always wins. Each model selected challenges designed to exploit its opponent’s weaknesses, scoring points only when it answered correctly and its opponent failed.


The results were surprising. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash won the heavyweight class despite not having the strongest answers. And GPT-6 Sol, the weakest model in that class by answer performance, won 17 of 20 matches against the strongest when both had access to scouting reports.


We analyzed the models’ decisions and identified five strategies. The most effective was to repeat a previous win against the same opponent. Models initially struggled to identify their opponents’ weaknesses, but improved as they accumulated evidence. Giving them a scouting report doubled the advantage they gained from their selections.


**The takeaway: An agent’s ability to make strategic decisions can matter as much as its ability to complete the underlying task.** Benchmarks measure what a model can do. They don’t necessarily measure how effectively it competes against another agent.


## Introduction


Most model benchmarks measure how well a model answers questions or completes tasks. But as agents increasingly interact with other agents, success may depend on more than their individual capabilities.


Consider a buyer’s agent negotiating with a seller’s agent, or a red-team agent testing another agent’s defenses. In both cases, understanding the other agent’s strengths and weaknesses can affect the outcome.


We wanted to understand how models make decisions in these competitive environments, and whether stronger performance on standalone tasks translates into winning against another model.


So we built a game where eight models competed in 954 cage matches, selecting challenges to gain an advantage over their opponents. We analyzed the strategies they developed, how those strategies changed as they learned about their opponents, and whether access to past performance data affected the results.


We found that the models with the strongest answers didn’t always win. In closely matched competitions, identifying and exploiting an opponent’s weaknesses could overcome an advantage in task performance.


## How we ran the cage matches


We designed a card game where eight models competed against one another by choosing challenges from a shared deck.


The deck contained 562 challenges across 17 categories, including logic puzzles, mathematics, coding, and tool use. Each model answered every challenge before the matches began. During the matches, models selected which challenges would count toward their scores rather than solving new problems.


Each match consisted of 30 rounds:


1. **Draw six cards.** Each card represented a challenge from a different category. Models could see the category and type of challenge, but not the question itself.
2. **Choose a card.** Both models independently selected one of the six challenges.
3. **Score the round.** A model earned a point when it had answered a selected challenge correctly and its opponent had answered incorrectly. If both models were correct or both were incorrect, neither earned points.
4. **Reveal the results.** Both models saw how they and their opponent had performed on all six challenges, including those neither selected.


Each model could also designate five of its selections per match as *triple cards* , worth three points instead of one.


We gave the models the rules, but no advice on how to win. Each model also had to explain its selection in two to four sentences, allowing us to analyze the strategies it reported using.


**Figure 1.** Round 2 of a match between DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GPT-6 Sol, with 2 triple cards. Only DeepSeek was correct on its tool-use card, so it won 3 points. The 2 models were correct on the card of Sol, so that card gave no points. After the round, the 2 models see the results of all 6 cards, also of the 4 cards that no model selected. **Figure 1.** Round 2 of a match between DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GPT-6 Sol, with 2 triple cards. Only DeepSeek was correct on its tool-use card, so it won 3 points. The 2 models were correct on the card of Sol, so that card gave no points. After the round, the 2 models see the results of all 6 cards, also of the 4 cards that no model selected.


### Dividing the models into weight classes


We began with a tournament in which every pair of models played 12 matches. The results revealed two distinct groups of four models, separated by approximately 250 Elo rating points.


Models in the stronger group won about nine out of ten matches against models in the weaker group. To make the competition more balanced, we divided them into two weight classes: heavyweight and middleweight.


Within each class, every model played 60 matches: 20 against each of the other three models.


**Figure 2.** The rating of the 8 models from the tournament, on the Elo scale, the rating scale of chess. A model with 100 rating points more than its opponent wins about 64% of their matches. The band shows the gap between the 2 weight classes: no model has a rating in it. The line through a dot shows 1 standard error. **Figure 2.** The rating of the 8 models from the tournament, on the Elo scale, the rating scale of chess. A model with 100 rating points more than its opponent wins about 64% of their matches. The band shows the gap between the 2 weight classes: no model has a rating in it. The line through a dot shows 1 standard error.


## Finding 1: The best answers don’t guarantee a win


DeepSeek V4.1 Flash won the heavyweight class, beating three closed models: Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol.


It won 39 of its 60 matches and finished first again in an additional series of 42 matches.


But DeepSeek didn’t have the strongest expected answer performance.


To separate task performance from strategic decision-making, we calculated how often each model would win if both opponents selected challenges at random. This gave us a baseline based on their answers alone, without any advantage from choosing particular challenges.


By that measure, Gemini 4 Argon was the strongest heavyweight model, with a 64% expected win rate. DeepSeek came second at 57%.


Yet in the actual matches, Gemini won only half its games, while DeepSeek won 39 out of 60.


**Figure 3.** Each model in its weight class. The open circle is the baseline, from the answers only: the win probability of a model if the 2 models select cards at random. The red dot is the result: its win probability in the played matches, where the models selected their cards. GPT-6 Sol, for example, goes from 29% to 43%. When the red dot has the higher value, the model won more than its answers alone predict. **Figure 3.** Each model in its weight class. The open circle is the baseline, from the answers only: the win probability of a model if the 2 models select cards at random. The red dot is the result: its win probability in the played matches, where the models selected their cards. GPT-6 Sol, for example, goes from 29% to 43%. When the red dot has the higher value, the model won more than its answers alone predict.


The difference was especially pronounced among closely matched models.


When models from different weight classes competed, the model with better answers won 91% of the time. But within the heavyweight class, that figure fell to just 61%.


GPT-6 Sol provides another example. It had the weakest answers of the heavyweight models, with an expected win probability of just 29% under random selection. Yet its strategic selections improved that probability to 43%, bringing it close to Gemini’s performance.


The middleweight class was different. Kimi K3.1 Pro, which had the strongest answers, also won the most matches. All four middleweight models finished in the same order as their underlying answer performance.


When differences in task capability were large, the stronger model usually won. But when capabilities were closer, the models’ decisions about which challenges to select could change the outcome.


We next looked at what those decisions had in common.


## Finding 2: Models developed five strategies. One dominated.


We gave the models no advice on how to win. But across thousands of decisions, patterns emerged in how they explained their choices.


We analyzed their stated reasons and identified five strategies:


Strategy What it is about What the model does In the words of a model Share of the decisions


**Repeat the win** Who solves the card The model was correct in this family of cards before, and its opponent was not. "On both previous 64-step state-tracking cards, I was correct and my opponent was wrong." (GPT-6 Sol) 59%


**Play my strength** Who solves the card The model expects a correct answer from itself. It does not compare with its opponent. "AIME problems have been reliable for me, though the opponent solves them too." (Claude Sonnet 5.5) 16%


**Guess a difference** Who solves the card The model has no such result. It guesses which card gives different results for the 2 models. "I choose the hard Code problem because I believe my coding ability gives me a comparative advantage over the opponent." (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) 12%


**Play the score** The score of the match The model is ahead and selects a safe card, or it is behind and takes a risk. "I lead 8-2, so I want low variance." (Claude Sonnet 5.5) 8%


**Attack a weak point** Who solves the card The model expects that its opponent fails, from the record or the name of its opponent only. "My opponent is a Flash-tier model, which may struggle more with hard, graduate-level calculation questions in Chemistry." (Gemini 4 Argon, about DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) 5%


**Table 1.** The 5 strategies that the models invented. Each quote is a part of a stated reason from a match of the tournament. The share is for the decisions of the weight-class matches.


One strategy dominated: **Repeat the win** .


We measured each strategy’s effectiveness by comparing the points earned from its selections with the expected points from selecting a card at random. Repeat the win accounted for 96% of the points models gained above random selection.


**Figure 4.** The gain of each strategy, in points for 10 selections. The gain of a selection is the points that its card wins above a random card of the same round. The percentage after the name of a strategy is its share of the decisions. A red bar is a gain, a gray bar is a loss, and the line shows 1 standard error. **Figure 4.** The gain of each strategy, in points for 10 selections. The gain of a selection is the points that its card wins above a random card of the same round. The percentage after the name of a strategy is its share of the decisions. A red bar is a gain, a gray bar is a loss, and the line shows 1 standard error.


The strategy worked because models earned points only when they answered correctly and their opponent failed. Choosing an easy challenge wasn’t enough if the opponent could solve it too.


By selecting challenges similar to ones they’d previously won, models could identify where they had an advantage. And because no challenge appeared twice, they had to apply that knowledge to new problems.


Other strategies were far less effective. Models that played to their own strengths often selected challenges their opponents could also solve. Others made assumptions based on an opponent’s reputation. Gemini 4 Argon, for example, chose a difficult chemistry challenge because it expected a “Flash-tier model” to struggle. Its opponent, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, answered correctly.


DeepSeek demonstrated the more successful approach in a match against GPT-6 Sol. After winning a tool-use challenge in round one, it selected two more challenges from the same family and assigned both triple-card bonuses. It won both, earning six points and ultimately winning the match.


As DeepSeek explained:


> In round 1, I answered Tool use correctly while my opponent was wrong, giving me a clear edge in this family.


The most effective strategy relied on demonstrated differences in performance, not assumptions about what either model should be good at.


## Finding 3: Knowing an opponent changes the game


In the first matches, models knew only their opponent’s name. They had to discover its strengths and weaknesses as the game progressed.


During the first five rounds, models selected challenges no better than random. Their decisions improved as they observed more results, with the advantage from their selections increasing until approximately round 20.


We wanted to see whether giving models information about their opponents upfront would change the outcome.


So we introduced *scouting reports* : records of how both models had performed on previous challenges. The reports contained no summaries or strategic advice, and excluded challenges from the upcoming match.


The effect was immediate. All eight models made better selections with scouting reports. Their advantage over random selection doubled, from 0.32 to 0.64 points per ten selections. With these records, models made effective decisions from the first round rather than spending most of the match learning about their opponents.


**Figure 5.** The gain of a selection in each part of a match, in points for 10 selections. The gray line is for the matches with no report: the gain starts near 0 and increases as a model sees more results. The red line is for the same matches with a report, and here the gain is high from the first rounds. After round 20, the 2 lines meet. **Figure 5.** The gain of a selection in each part of a match, in points for 10 selections. The gray line is for the matches with no report: the gain starts near 0 and increases as a model sees more results. The red line is for the same matches with a report, and here the gain is high from the first rounds. After round 20, the 2 lines meet.


When only one model had a scouting report, its estimated win probability rose from 50% to 66%.


### The weakest heavyweight model beat the strongest 17 times out of 20


Gemini 4 Argon had the strongest expected answer performance in the heavyweight class, while GPT-6 Sol had the weakest. Yet when both models had scouting reports, Sol won 17 of their 20 matches, compared with 12 without them.


Sol identified a weakness in Gemini’s performance on state-tracking challenges. Sol had 96% accuracy on these challenges, compared with Gemini’s 52%.


With scouting reports, Sol allocated 79 of its 100 triple-card selections across their matches to state tracking, up from 50 without them.


As Sol explained in one match:


> On prior 64-step state-tracking challenges, I was consistently correct while my opponent was often wrong.


**Figure 6.** Each model in its weight class, in the matches with a scouting report. The open circle is the same baseline as in Figure 3: the win probability if the 2 models select cards at random. The red dot is the win probability with the report. In each class, the models are in the order of their answers, with the best answers first. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash won the heavy class again. In the middle class, the stronger model still won most of the matches. **Figure 6.** Each model in its weight class, in the matches with a scouting report. The open circle is the same baseline as in Figure 3: the win probability if the 2 models select cards at random. The red dot is the win probability with the report. In each class, the models are in the order of their answers, with the best answers first. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash won the heavy class again. In the middle class, the stronger model still won most of the matches.


Across the heavyweight class, the model with better answers won just 51% of matches when both competitors had scouting reports, compared with 61% without them.


The additional information didn’t make models better at answering questions. It helped them identify which questions gave them the greatest advantage.


## What this means for multi-agent systems


As agents increasingly interact with other agents, standalone benchmarks may not tell the whole story. Our findings suggest three implications for engineers:


1. **Test agents against their opponents.** Standalone task performance doesn’t necessarily predict how an agent will perform against another agent.
2. **Give agents access to past results.** Even simple records of previous interactions can help agents identify and exploit an opponent’s weaknesses.
3. **Examine how agents make decisions.** Understanding the strategies behind their choices can reveal weaknesses that task-success metrics miss.


**The strongest model doesn’t always win. How effectively an agent learns and adapts to its opponent can change the outcome.**

In a match, no model answers a challenge: the game draws 1 saved answer of each model for each card. For a win probability, we kept the selected cards of a match, and we drew the saved answers again 800 times or more.
